Introduction & Executive Summary** #### **1.1 Introduction** At the time of writing of the previous edition of Quarterly Copper Forecast in February, the global economic backdrop was in dire straits and sentiment was probably at its lowest. The outlook for base metals at the time seemed bleak, with prices having just come off multi-year lows and all the relevant forward looking indicators pointing to conditions worsening further. GFMS Metals Consulting expected that in 2009, copper consumption in developed countries would suffer material losses while growth in developing countries was seen falling notably from recent years’ levels. As results for the first few months of the year emerged, these expectations have indeed been confirmed. The principal difference between the projections featured in the previous edition of this report lies in production. In February, we had expected the abovementioned weakness of copper consumption would occur against the backdrop of higher refined output. The latest production data from the International Copper Study Group as well as ongoing indications that mine production is under pressure had led us to revise some of our earlier assumptions. Refined production in 2008 for instance seems to have increased by less than 2% to 18.282m tonnes. We expect that this year grow

th will be marginal. As a result, although the weak demand conditions do indeed see a market in surplus, the extent of this surplus is far lower than we had initially expected. Another important point to note is that, to-date, net increases in stocks seem to have largely been centred in China, with LME stocks at end-May being lower than at the end of last year. Even taking into consideration purchases by the SRB, the surge in imports so far this year points to a build of unreported inventories in China. Chinese copper demand has benefited from the government’s stimulus package. For example, copper semis production in the first four months of the year was up by just over 10%. Improved conditions in the Chinese market are also reflected in the country’s manufacturing PMI, which showed expansion for the third consecutive month in May. Moreover, although Figure 1.1

As a result of all the above, GFMS Metals Consulting has revised its projections on copper supply and (to a lesser extent) demand for the 2009-2011 period. In addition, we have extended our forecast to 2012. O

ur forecasts are discussed in the relevant section of this chapter and in yet more detail in the relevant chapters on consumption and production. #### **1.2 Market background** Although copper prices were among the last of the base metals to peak at $8,985/tonne on July 3 2008, the performance since then has been remarkably similar to the rest of the sector. Over the six months following the peak, copper prices gave up the bulk of their gains, falling to a low of $2,770/tonne in December. This year-to-date and particularly from March onwards, prices have recovered to current levels around $5,000. As we have discussed in our previous research, the main theme in the copper market has been the battle between tight supply and the weak demand environment. Recent revisions to the 2008 production estimates illustrate that the former remains a feature of the market, with examples being the grade problems keeping Chilean output low and African Copper-belt production once again failing to live up to potential. Regarding the latter, despite recent talk of “green sprouts”, particularly in China, demand remains weak across all the key markets for copper. For much of the recent bear market, LME inventories increased notably. Recently, these have collapsed to levels lower than those at the end of last year. Although this may create the illusion that the market is entering a deficit, we remain cautious towards this conjecture and believe that rather than an actual drain on stocks, the decline largely reflects a move from LME warehouses and into unreported stocks in China. Nevertheless, the low level of LME inventories (at endMay they represented a little over one week’s Western World consumption), is undoubtedly supportive of higher prices. Figures 1.1 and 1.3 highlight trends in both LME and total reported stocks versus the price. In Figure 1.2, we highlight the position of copper compared to the other metals. As discussed later in this chapter, even taking into account our forecast surpluses for 2009 and 2010, the stock build is not excessive from a historical stand point, which is another factor to make us positive about the long-term prospects for the metal. #### **1.3 Economic assumptions** GFMS Metals Consulting’s expectations on the way the global economy will develop over the course of the forecast period are central to our expectations on copper supply, demand and prices. In line with the rest of our forecast work, we present our projections in three scenarios, dubbed Base Case, reflecting what we consider the most likely outcome and Scenario B (higher copper prices) and Scenario C (lower copper prices). **Base case:** Real global GDP growth under our Base Case Scenario (weighted with a 40% probability outcome) is forecast to turn negative in 2009, to -1.5%. The first quarter results show a number of key western markets are deep into recession and Chinese growth having slowed to 6.1%. Although, as noted in the introduction, a number of forward looking indicators are turning positive, we feel that we are some way from a recovery commencing. As the latter unfolds from late 2009 and notably in 2010, we see growth turn positive next year, accelerating in the last two years of the forecast period. ###### **~~Figure 1.5~~** LME Stocks vs Monthly Average Price

The massive cash injections and other initiatives taken by major governments and central banks have a more immediate impact on markets, boosting lending and reigniting an economic recovery that sees global GDP rise by 0.9% in real terms this year, increasing notably over the course of the forecast period. Inherent in this scenario is also far stronger inflation, the result of “quantitative easing” policies being maintained for a longer period and a more aggressive debt monetisation than under the base case. **Scenario C:** (weighted with a 25% probability outcome). The central theme of the final, least likely in our view, scenario is what one could term ‘liquidity trap’. Despite the efforts of monetary and fiscal authorities to boost money supply and encourage borrowing, these initiatives fail to translate in rising property, equity and commodity prices. Economic recovery is delayed and its momentum weak. Global GDP contracts by an extra-ordinary 2.1% in 2009 and growth is lacklustre next year, at 0.6%. Going forward, as we see the massive intervention in the US economy will likely see the country recover faster than other markets (importantly the Eurozone), and our Base Case sees the dollar strengthening over the rest of the forecast period against the euro, despite the easing seen in late May. #### **1.4 The funds** Although the involvement of speculative investors in commodity markets has declined considerably compared to the levels seen through to the middle of last year, their impact on prices remains considerable. One should to remember that, being relatively shallow, at least compared with financial markets, modest volumes of activity can at times have a material impact on prices and liquidity. As GFMS Metals Consulting has often noted, it is next to impossible to provide a meaningful estimate of the impact of investor activity on the copper market (and indeed, all base metals). Aside from the limited information contained in LME Open Interest and non-commercial and non-reportable net positions in Comex futures, one can largely only rely on anecdotal evidence of trends in the market. As mentioned in the introductory section of this chapter, this year-todate investor attitudes towards copper have improved materially and we feel this has certainly contributed to the price recovery. Going forward, we expect this will continue, initially due to the tightness of supply and eventually on the back of a rebound in consumption, as the global economy moves into a sustainable recovery. Our expectations on how this impacts prices under each of the three scenarios are provided later in this chapter. #### **1.5 Consumption** Two important points to remember about copper demand trends are that aside from the emergence of China as the largest and fastest growing source of demand in this decade, there has been little overall change in average annual growth rates. Indeed, excluding China, global consumption declined by an annual average 0.4% over the 2000-2008 period. Our figure is somewhat distorted by the exceptionally high base in 200

0, the result of the dot-com bubble. Since the second half of last year in particular, consumption has been under considerable pressure, until recently even in countries like China. Consumption growth in the latter, for instance, was a mere 4.9% last year and were it not for SRB purchases of 300,000 tonnes we have assumed will take place over the year, our projections see consumption growing by 8.7% in 2009, despite the very aggressive stimulus package underway, expected to boost demand in the second half of the year. Elsewhere, the majority of short term indicators that we track such as premiums, shipments data on copper semis, company production data for copper fabricators, as well as the economic data, although perhaps off their lows recorded earlier in the year, continue to point to relatively weak demand conditions. We still hold the view that the subdued demand conditions will remain in place for the bulk of 2009. Towards the end of the year, we expect the extraordinary measures implemented by governments will begin to “kick-in”. In spite of the support this is forecast to provide the market and the Chinese reserve purchases, we forecast that in 2009 overall, global consumption will fall by 0.8%. As the industrial production recovers in 2010 and also boosted by the stocking cycle, consumption is expected to grow by an impressive 7.4% y-o-y. A return to more “normal” rates of growth (6.4% and 5.2% respectively) is then forecast for the last two years of the forecast period.

Coupled with the handful of price-related cutbacks underway, we forecast this will leave mine production in 2009 down 0.8% y-o-y. Following this, we expect that as some of these disruptions are overcome and boosted by expansions in capacity elsewhere, production will rise a healthy 6.4% annually on average, over the rest of the forecast period. Moving to refining, we continue to see no bottlenecks on that stage of production. Refining capacity is set to continue growing throughout the world, spear-headed by China. Refining capacity is set to receive additional boost by the growing share SX-EW output is expected to account of global production. Refined output is expected to be virtually flat this year, as concentrates’ stocks are drawn on to compensate for declining mine production and a tight scrap market. The growth of SX-EW output will boost the bottom line. Fol

lowing that, output is projected to grow by an annual average 4.8% over the course of the rest of the forecast period.  (The difference between mine production growth and refined production growth primarily reflects the replenishment of ‘normal’ levels of concentrate stocks at refineries.) 

#### **1.7 Market outlook** 

##### **1.7.1 Base case scenario** 

Given the latest revisions to ICSG consumption and production statistics for 2008, the copper market seems to have been in surplus of 276,000 tonnes over the year.  GFMS Metals Consulting expect this will continue this year, with oversupply increasing to 441,000 tonnes. Given the recent collapse in LME inventories this may seem surprisingly pessimistic.  Moreover, one could make the argument that it contradicts the relatively benign outlook implied in the $4,230 average copper price we forecast for 2009 overall. 

Regarding the size of the surplus we forecast for the year, careful examination of the key components of supply and demand can shed some light.  Starting with consumption, despite allowing for 300,000 tonnes of Chinese SRB purchases and improved ‘real’ consumption growth in the country, expected declines elsewhere (notably Western Europe, Japan and the United States) have dragged the global figure into negative growth.  Although refined production is also under pressure, as a result of falling mine production, our projections see it essentially flat y-o-y, suggesting the gap between that and demand will increase. 

Considering LME stocks, although we expect these will eventually recover later in the year, we would not be surprised to see the net inflow into these falling significantly short of the size of the surplus.  Anecdotal evidence and our view of Chinese consumption, coupled with strong imports, suggest that this year-to-date unreported stocks in the country have grown materially, and this is likely to continue for much of the rest of the year.
